study.title: Ezekiel 2 - Call, sending and the scroll of the divine message
study.overview: Ezekiel is erected by the Spirit to receive a difficult mission: to speak in the name of the Lord to a rebellious people. The chapter shows that the prophet does not speak on his own initiative, but as a messenger sent by God, without depending on the reaction of the public. The view of the scroll concludes the scene by drawing attention to the content of the message: laments, sighs and si, that is, judgment against the rebellion and urgency of repentance.

outline.title: The Prophet is raised and sent
outline.explanation: God sends Ezekiel to stand, and the Spirit enables him to obey. Then the prophet receives his commission to go to the children of Israel, described as rebels who have resisted God for a long time.

outline.title: A word to a rebellious house
outline.explanation: Ezekiel must announce, "Thus says the Lord GOD." He must not fear the hardness of the people or measure their success by the response received. His responsibility is to faithfully speak the words of God, whether the people hear, or refuse to hear.

outline.title: The roll of the message of judgment
outline.explanation: God commands the prophet to listen and receive the word without rebellion. Then appears a scroll written on both sides, a sign of great fullness of the message, containing lamentations, sighs, and ais, that is, oracles of judgment and pain.

study.context: The text presents the prophetic vocation as a direct call of God, not as a human career or automatic family inheritance. The notes highlight that Ezekiel receives this submission while standing before the divine glory and that the division of the chapter fits with the closure of the previous vision. The public mentioned is the home of Israel in a condition of rebellion, and the language points to the need to announce a severe message to a resilient people.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the authority of the prophetic message comes from God, not the messenger. The Spirit empowers Ezekiel for obedience and service, showing that divine mission requires spiritual dependence. There is also a strong contrast between Israel's rebellion and the expected obedience of the prophet: he must not imitate the hardness of the people, but to receive the word and convey it faithfully. Theologically, judgment is not a secondary detail, but a central part of God's message before the broken covenant. At the same time, the fact that the people "know that there was a prophet among them" indicates that God bears clear testimony of his word, even when it is rejected. The scene of the scroll highlights the integrity and extent of the divine message: it is complete, heavy and focused on confrontation with sin.

scholarViews.insight: The prophetic call is not an inherited occupation; God raises Ezekiel by the Spirit and sends him to a rebellious people, so that he may be a sign of hope and obedience.
The chapter shows Ezekiel's ordination for prophetic service: he must not only contemplate the vision, but enter into action as a minister sent to the people.
The scroll written inside and outside represents the fullness of the messages of judgment that Ezekiel should announce to a rebellious people.

questions: What changes in our reading of Ezekiel's mission when we realize that it is born of God's sending, not human initiative?
In what ways does the order not to fear the people confront the tendency to measure ministry only by immediate results?
How does the image of the scroll full of lamentations, sighs and size help us to take sin and divine judgment seriously?
study.practice: Apply this chapter by examining whether your posture before the Word is submission or resistance. Pray that God may give you the Spirit to listen, obey and speak faithfully, without fear of opposition. If you advertise or teach the Bible, remember that your task is to convey God's message clearly, even when it is not well received. And, as a reader, allow the seriousness of judgment to lead to repentance and concrete obedience, not just to intellectual knowledge.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are summarized and are in English; therefore, some ideas have been synthesized in Portuguese without enlarging beyond what they claim. Adam Clarke's note in v. 10 was truncated in the received excerpt, so the description of the scroll was limited to what appears explicitly in the excerpt and the biblical text. There is also no safe data, in the notes provided, to develop additional historical details beyond what the chapter itself and the comments mention.
